title: Freezing injunctions are outrunning the tracing work behind them
author: Claire Duffield
snippet: 2 days ago … Got a worldwide freezing order last month. By the time it was served, two thirds of the balance had already moved through a cross-chain bridge. The order was sound; the intelligence underneath it was three weeks stale …
reason: A disputes lawyer describing the gap between legal relief and forensic timing — our strongest referral audience.

comments.text: The sequencing matters more than most orders acknowledge: once funds cross a bridge, the relevant respondent is often a different exchange in a different jurisdiction than the one named. Tracing before the application rather than after changes who you name.

When the order was served, did you have current attribution on the destination cluster, or was it based on the position at filing? The gap between those two dates is usually where recovery is won or lost.

We see the same pattern — the legal instrument is fine, the underlying picture is weeks old. Refreshing attribution immediately before service is unglamorous, and it is often what makes the order enforceable.

title: Non-disclosure in financial remedy cases now has a wallet-shaped hole in it
author: Petra Zalar
snippet: 4 days ago … Family practitioners are getting comfortable asking about crypto on Form E, but asking is not the same as knowing what to do with a wallet address once you have one. Two cases this year turned on whether a disclosed address actually held the value …
reason: Family law practitioner naming a concrete procedural gap where forensic input is decisive.

comments.text: A disclosed address is a starting point, not an answer — it is common for it to be a spending account while value sits one hop away in a cluster the same party controls. Clustering is what turns disclosure into evidence.
In those two cases, did the discrepancy surface from the respondent's own disclosure or from exchange records obtained separately? The route matters for how others should frame their requests.

The pattern we see most in financial remedy work is not a hidden wallet but a disclosed one that is deliberately empty. Asking for full transaction history rather than a balance closes most of that gap.

title: Source of funds checks on crypto are still mostly assertion with a screenshot attached
author: Daniel Weiss
snippet: 1 week ago … Reviewed a stack of SoF files this quarter. Most consisted of an exchange balance screenshot and a customer explanation. That is not provenance. Regulators are going to start asking what sits behind the screenshot …
reason: A compliance lead describing precisely the trigger for source-of-funds work.

comments.text: The distinction worth drawing in a file is between where funds are now and where they demonstrably came from. A balance screenshot evidences custody at a point in time and nothing about origin — only one of those is the regulator's question.
Are you seeing pressure to evidence provenance across the full chain history, or only back to the last fiat on-ramp? That scope question seems to be where institutions are landing very differently.

Where files hold up under scrutiny, it is usually because someone reconstructed the path forward from the on-ramp rather than working backwards from the current balance. Slower, and the part that survives review.

title: MiCA supervision is about to become a data problem, not a licensing one
author: Ilaria Fontana
snippet: 5 days ago … Most of the market still treats MiCA as an authorisation exercise. The harder phase starts after: supervisors will want ongoing analytics, and very few CASPs have the pipeline to produce them on request …
reason: Regulatory piece whose audience overlaps heavily with our compliance buyers.

comments.text: The shift changes what compliance teams need to keep: authorisation rewards a point-in-time file, ongoing supervision rewards a reproducible pipeline. Those imply different tooling and usually different staff.
Do you expect supervisors to converge on a common analytics format, or is the realistic near-term outcome that each national authority asks for something slightly different?
The firms least anxious about this are the ones that already had to answer an investigative request under time pressure. Doing it once exposes whether the underlying data is actually queryable.

title: The 24-hour NIS2 notification is not the hard part
author: Bojan Kralj
snippet: 3 days ago … Everyone is drilling the initial notification. The pain arrives at the one-month final report, when you are asked what actually happened and the forensic work was never scoped to answer that …
reason: CISO-level post on the seam between incident response and regulatory reporting.

comments.text: Scoping forensic work to the eventual report rather than to containment is what makes the one-month deadline survivable. Containment answers whether it stopped; the report asks what happened, and only one of those is evidenced by default.
Are you seeing organisations pull the reporting obligation into the IR retainer itself, or does it still land on legal after the fact?
The final report is usually where teams discover which logs rotated on day three. Setting retention against the reporting deadline rather than the investigation is a cheap fix, made far too late.
